Josh Shapiro sets out his foreign-policy priorities ahead of expected 2028 run, and U.S. to hit China, other nations with fresh sanctions     JONATHAN ERNST/REUTERS   Good morning. President Trump’s rescue of Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang, which has incensed Republicans and Democrats on Capitol Hill, apparently isn’t the first time he has rushed to save a tech CEO.

   Trump disclosed in a Monday CNBC interview that he had “protected” Elon Musk in his first term, though he didn’t detail how.

   “I protected Elon in my first term, very big. Elon was protected. I talk about it, and I’m proud of Elon. I love Elon. I think he’s great. You know, 80% supergenius, 20% he has other problems, but I tell him that. But Elon I protected. You wouldn’t have an Elon if it wasn’t for me, and with that certain incident that took place, which was, you know, a tough incident.”

   Trump didn’t go into more detail, but he did say “we have to protect our brilliant people because we don’t have enough.”

   Musk had some tangles with the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term, but it’s hard to imagine that a Trump intervention in those cases might have saved Elon’s entire career. (Perhaps coincidentally, the SEC chairman during that time was Jay Clayton, who is now Trump’s director of national intelligence and has played a role in the Huang matter).

   Trump’s explanation sounded a bit like what he told journalist Bob Woodward in a tape-recorded 2020 interview about how he claimed to have protected Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

   “I saved his a—,” Trump told Woodward. “That’s what happened.”

   Woodward asked Trump whose “a—” was saved.

   “MBS. They were coming down on him very strongly. But I was able to get Congress to leave him alone.”

   Huang is headed to Congress next week for at least two appearances before lawmakers. Unless things change, he will be met by the sound and the fury of Capitol Hill. It could test how far Trump’s protection extends.

The U.S. is preparing to impose fresh levies on China and dozens of other countries that the Trump administration argues are harming American companies by supporting their own domestic industrial production. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer is expected to unveil the results of a tariff probe into the industrial subsidies of China, the European Union and 14 other nations.

Trump Says He Protects ‘Brilliant’ CEOs Like Elon Musk and Jensen Huang
 
Plus, Gov. Josh Shapiro sets out his foreign-policy priorities ahead of expected 2028 run, and U.S. to hit China, other nations with fresh sanctions
 
 
JONATHAN ERNST/REUTERS
 

Good morning. President Trump’s rescue of Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang, which has incensed Republicans and Democrats on Capitol Hill, apparently isn’t the first time he has rushed to save a tech CEO.

 

Trump disclosed in a Monday CNBC interview that he had “protected” Elon Musk in his first term, though he didn’t detail how.

 

“I protected Elon in my first term, very big. Elon was protected. I talk about it, and I’m proud of Elon. I love Elon. I think he’s great. You know, 80% supergenius, 20% he has other problems, but I tell him that. But Elon I protected. You wouldn’t have an Elon if it wasn’t for me, and with that certain incident that took place, which was, you know, a tough incident.”

 

Trump didn’t go into more detail, but he did say “we have to protect our brilliant people because we don’t have enough.”

 

Musk had some tangles with the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term, but it’s hard to imagine that a Trump intervention in those cases might have saved Elon’s entire career. (Perhaps coincidentally, the SEC chairman during that time was Jay Clayton, who is now Trump’s director of national intelligence and has played a role in the Huang matter).

 

Trump’s explanation sounded a bit like what he told journalist Bob Woodward in a tape-recorded 2020 interview about how he claimed to have protected Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

 

“I saved his a—,” Trump told Woodward. “That’s what happened.”

 

Woodward asked Trump whose “a—” was saved.

 

“MBS. They were coming down on him very strongly. But I was able to get Congress to leave him alone.”

 

Huang is headed to Congress next week for at least two appearances before lawmakers. Unless things change, he will be met by the sound and the fury of Capitol Hill. It could test how far Trump’s protection extends.

What I’m Following

 
 
DAVID ZALUBOWSKI/AP
 

A 2028 contender for the Democrats, Josh Shapiro sets out his foreign policy. The Pennsylvania governor, who has garnered significant presidential buzz in recent months, called on Trump to end the Iran war, described the president’s talks with Russia as “an embarrassment to our country,” and said the U.S. needs to clamp down on chip exports to China.

 

China and dozens of other countries to be hit with new U.S. tariffs. The U.S. is preparing to impose fresh levies on China and dozens of other countries that the Trump administration argues are harming American companies by supporting their own domestic industrial production. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer is expected to unveil the results of a tariff probe into the industrial subsidies of China, the European Union and 14 other nations.

 

A Democratic push for Medicare for All is already narrowing in scope. Lawmakers and those coming into office are watering down their plans given the high cost of Medicare expansions and obstacles to reworking a private health-insurance market that covers more than 200 million Americans.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• The CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence said some unclassified information was exposed in a cybersecurity breach.

 

• Huang apologized during an Nvidia town-hall staff meeting, saying he is in therapy.

 

• Just 65.6% of newborns received the hepatitis B vaccine in the first half of 2026 after a federal panel ended recommendations for the shot last winter.
